meta.title: NYC’s Urban Textscape
meta.description: Analyzing All of the Words Found on NYC Streets
meta.byline: Data by Yufeng Zhao. Story by Matt Daniels

slides.text: What if you could search every visible word on New York City’s streets?
First, we’d need to transcribe every business sign, bumper sticker, ad, flyer—anything with text.
All these transcribed words are a wealth of information: non-English text could indicate a cultural enclave, like this one in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.
We can pinpoint the phrases that comprise NYC vernacular.
From everyday common words…
…to phrases that uniquely blanket the city.
If you know, you know.

section.value: This is possible because media artist Yufeng Zhao fed millions of panoramas from Google Street View into a computer program that transcribes text within the images.

The result is a search engine of much of what’s written in NYC’s streets. It's limited to what a Google Street View car can capture, so it excludes text in areas like alleyways and parks, or any writing too small to be read by a moving vehicle.
The scale of the data is immense: over 8 million Google Streetview images (from the past 18 years) and 138 million identified snippets of text.
The resulting data is truly astonishing; it feels like sifting through the city's source code. For example, here's all 111,290 matches for “pizza,” on a map.
Let's look at some other maps.

slides.text: Matches for “Broadway” identify street signs, of course. The resulting map is also oddly satisfying: it reveals a constellation that illuminates Broadway in each of the five boroughs’.
slides.title: Broadway

slides.text: Zooming into Times Square, “Broadway” expands to depict Broadway theaters.
Every new residential building calls itself “luxury,” but only Hudson Yards has applied the label to an entire neighborhood.
slides.title: Luxury

slides.text: There's a simple answer to why “beware” has such a clear geographic footprint, oddly completely absent from Manhattan. At the end of this article, we’ll show you why that is, or you can get a hint…
slides.title: Beware

slides.text: The map of “gold” depicts Manhattan’s Diamond District, as well as streets lined with “we buy gold” jewelry and pawn shops.
slides.title: Gold

slides.text: Some of the more interesting maps depict cultural enclaves. Coordinates for “iglesia” (church, in Spanish) indicate Spanish-speaking communities.
slides.title: Iglesia

slides.text: Similarly, jerk (the cooking style, not the personality) points to Jamaican enclaves in Flatbush, Brooklyn and Jamaica (the neighborhood) in Queens.
slides.title: Jerk

slides.text: See if you can guess this one, based on the geography: this adjective denotes that it’s not just a barbershop and not just a salon.

section.value: The actually Streetview imagery is also revealing. With a simple search, we can see how these words appear on NYC streets.

slides.text: First, here’s probably the most Brooklyn phrase ever, which actually appears on signs as you exit the borough.
slides.title: Fuhgeddaboudit

slides.text: We were able to capture most graffiti text (and tags!)—anything visible from the street.
slides.title: Acab

slides.text: Some text was temporary, but indefinitely memorialized in Google Streetview (these images are from 2020-2023).
slides.title: Covid

section.value: Most of the data is what you would expect. “Stop” is the #1 word in the dataset, appearing 1,304,417 times, followed by “One way.” No surprises there. But a few phrases are background noise to most people, and once you see it, you can’t unsee it.

slides.text: First, here are the most common words, as well as phrases in our data (the algorithm identified phrases if they appeared as a single line of text).
As expected, many of these are related to driving, traffic, and street signs, words that you’d find on any streetscape in the US.
Let’s filter these out, as well as common filler words (as, the, is, of, etc.), so we can explore the more surprising terms that appear in NYC.
Fedders, at #28, is the logo of an A/C brand that had their units built into the exterior of buildings, from the 1950s to the 1990s, as through-the-wall slots.
slides.post: The logo is so common that houses adorned with the phrase have earned the name “Fedders houses,” a pejorative for “reviled” post-WW2 construction. They don’t make A/C units for this integrated design anymore, so the ubiquitous Fedders logo is the result of people leaving the decade-old Fedders-branded metal cover on the obsolete A/C slot.

slides.text: At #122 is Yodock, a brand of orange and white plastic barriers, often seen in make-shift sidewalks around construction areas.
Acars (at #289) is actually “4cars,” misread by our algorithm for translating text in images. The Cash4Cars signs are (illegally) affixed to street signs and lamp posts throughout the city.
slides.post: Apparently in 2021, the Staten Island District Attorney arrested at least one of the men behind the operation on issued 62 summonses.

slides.text: Nathan’s might have the hot dog brand cachet, but Sabrett (ranking 336th) has the territory, with carts in most NYC tourist traps.
slides.post: Apparently you can rent a Sabrett cart for your next event!

slides.text: NYC is home to largest Muslim community in the United States, so it’s no surprise to see halal— food prepared according to Islamic dietary law—ranked at #351.
slides.post: Halal carts started in the 1980s and are now a staple NYC street food, so much so that NYC mayoral Democratic party nominee Zohran Mamdani campaigned on this relatability with his “halalflation” promise: to lower the cost of chicken over rice by $2.

slides.text: Siamese (#404) refers to a type of hose connection for firefighters. More modern (and less racially-charged) names include FDC (Fire Department Connection) and standpipe connection.

Earlier, we depicted the geography of beware (#444), which is concentrated in residential areas fortunate enough to have lawns and fencing. Here we see how popular the phrase is, ranking in the top 1,000.

In case you didn’t already know, you’re practically always under surveillance (#587) in NYC. The NYPD, businesses, developers, and even the Parks Department are more than happy to remind you they're recording.
